final_answer: When an mRNA vaccine is injected, it enters muscle cells near the injection site. The mRNA contains instructions for making a harmless piece of the virus’s spike protein. The cells use this mRNA to produce the spike protein, which is then displayed on their surface. The immune system detects this protein as foreign, triggering the production of antibodies and activating T cells. These immune responses create memory cells that recognize and fight the actual virus if encountered later. Importantly, the mRNA does not enter the cell’s nucleus, so it does not alter DNA. The body breaks down the mRNA after use, ensuring no long-term effects.
